subject: Nariway Signals - 2026-08-29 - a founder's will, ignored by his own foundation
html:
Nariway Signals
Saturday, August 29, 2026
Heaviest today on the gap between what a founder wanted and what the people left holding a collection actually do — Robert Indiana’s own foundation selling the house his will designated a future public art space, right as Yayoi Kusama’s museum admits two weeks on that it has no named successor, bracketed by a third European museum heist in as many weeks and a UK export bar keeping a $97M Rembrandt from leaving the country.
Lead
Robert Indiana’s own foundation is selling the house his will said should become a public art space
Indiana’s will directed that the Star of Hope — the 19th-century Odd Fellows lodge on Vinalhaven, Maine, where he lived and worked for 40 years — be restored “to museum quality” and opened to the public for visits, classes and lectures. The Star of Hope Foundation, the body he set up to carry that out, is instead listing the building for $1.4M and a second property for $210K; board chair Emily Lane says the proceeds go toward “artistic and cultural initiatives on Vinalhaven” rather than the building itself. It’s the plainest live instance yet of the donor-intent tension this brief keeps tracking — Ty Warner’s naming-rights suit, the Berkshire and Orlando Museum fights, the Phillips Collection’s redrawn “core collection” — a founder’s own written wishes losing out to the practical judgment of the people entrusted to execute them.

ARTnews → · Bangor Daily News →
What’s happening
Yayoi Kusama’s museum still hasn’t named a successor, two weeks after her death
The Kusama Museum and studio in Tokyo say her mission will be “carried forward,” but the continuity statement names no successor leader and sets out no policy for unfinished works, archive access, authentication, or future refabrications of her Infinity Mirror Rooms — an open governance question sitting directly under one of the most commercially valuable living-artist markets right as it becomes a legacy one.
The Art Newspaper →
A Vienna museum theft, the third this brief has logged in two weeks
Two men bought tickets, smashed a display case with a hammer, and walked out of the Museum of Applied Arts with a 200-carat, 673-diamond Van Cleef & Arpels necklace made for Princess Fawzia of Egypt’s 1939 wedding — worth over $4M and the city’s most valuable art theft since the 2003 Cellini Saliera heist. Coming a day after Villena’s Bronze Age hoard and a week after Europol’s report on museum heists turning more violent, it’s the same story a third time: European museum security is being tested in real time, right when this brief’s insurance-and-stewardship conversation needs it least.
CBS News → · Bloomberg →
The UK just gave a Rembrandt the most valuable “national treasure” export bar on record
Portrait of Catrina Hooghsaet (1657), sold in a private sale via Christie’s last year for a reported £71M ($97M), has been placed under a temporary UK export bar — the most expensive object ever to receive the designation — giving a UK institution or collector a window to match the price and keep it in the country. A useful data point on how a private sale, not an auction, is now where the biggest single-work moves happen, and on how much national governments will now spend defending against exactly that.
The Art Newspaper → · Artnet →
Powerhouse Parramatta’s CEO has stood aside, ten weeks before the museum’s Nov 7 opening
Lisa Havilah, who has led the A$915M Sydney project since 2018, stepped back Aug 27 amid a New South Wales government investigation into governance and procurement; the opening date itself is unchanged, with a former Sydney Opera House chief executive brought in as strategic advisor. A leadership shakeout at exactly the moment this brief has been tracking the museum’s opening countdown as one of the year’s biggest public-museum builds.
The Art Newspaper →
Worth reading
Roland-Philippe Kretzschmar, “The Best Defence of the Mega-Galleries Has Nothing To Do With Money” (The Art Bystander)
Pitched first to Artnet, published here after they declined a back-and-forth: Kretzschmar argues the mega-galleries “are turning into institutions, taking over ground museums can no longer afford to hold” — and that this isn’t the scandal it’s usually framed as. A sharp companion to every collector-museum this brief tracks: if the gallery is becoming the institution, the founder-museum stops being the only serious legacy vehicle in town.
The Art Bystander →
Barry W. Finkelstein, “What to Do When Collections Outlive Their Owners” (Trusts & Estates)
A practicing estate-planning attorney’s case study of a successor trustee administering an 82-year-old Silicon Valley executive’s estate — 26 vehicles, automobilia, a ski lodge, an apartment building, and art — walking through valuation, distribution, and the practical chaos of a collection nobody planned an exit for. About as concrete as the trusts-and-estates trade press gets on exactly Nariway’s question.
WealthManagement.com →
“Federal Estate and Income Tax Issues Affecting Artwork Located in the United States at Death” (WealthManagement.com, Aug 21)
A practitioner-facing walkthrough of the tax mechanics that kick in the moment a US-situated collection changes hands at death — useful ballast alongside the Finkelstein piece above for anyone advising a family through exactly that moment.
WealthManagement.com →
To see
Christie’s Alan Medaugh Hiroshige preview is now 13 days out
Public preview Sept 11–14, sale Sept 15, 20 Rockefeller Plaza — already on the calendar for the Sept 12 preview.
ARTnews →
Sotheby’s Open House (Sept 20–21) is now 22 days out
Its confirmed program includes a session on legal considerations across an art collection’s lifecycle, staged by the house’s own trusts-and-estates practice.
Sotheby’s →
For the record
Rotterdam’s Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen is caught up in a municipal bribery scandal
Two city employees have been fired after an investigation found they took bribes in exchange for approving inflated construction contracts, including asbestos-removal work at the museum; the city reportedly paid millions too much for the cleanup as a result. A reminder that a museum’s own building maintenance is itself a place institutional stewardship can quietly fail.
